text: Every shot, the plastic in this mould stays molten, right up to the part. Nothing to cut off, nothing to regrind.
Here's how a hot runner does it, and how it fails.
The hot runner.
In a cold runner mould, the plastic in the runner freezes with the part, and is thrown away or reground every cycle.
A hot runner keeps that plastic molten. The machine nozzle feeds a heated sprue, then a manifold: a steel block with flow channels drilled through it.
Heaters wrap the manifold, and its channels split the melt evenly, so every cavity sees the same pressure and temperature.
From the manifold, the melt runs down heated nozzles, to a gate at each cavity.
Every heater has its own thermocouple. Each pair is a zone, and a controller holds every zone at its set point, often within a degree.
The nozzle tip is the hard part. It must keep the plastic hot inside, while the steel around the gate is cooled, so the part can freeze.
Some gates are thermal: a plug of plastic freezes at the tip between shots. Others are valve gates, where a pin driven by air or oil closes the gate.
The manifold floats in an air gap, touching the mould only at a few small points, so its heat stays where the melt is.
And here's the clever part. The seal between manifold and nozzle is made by heat.
As the manifold warms up, it grows, and presses down on the nozzles. Cold, there's a gap. Hot, it seals.
A nozzle can reach temperature in about three minutes, but it needs roughly fifteen more to grow to full size. A manifold can take half an hour, plus soak time.
But a hot runner punishes shortcuts.
Inject before the system has soaked, and the seal isn't made. Melt is forced out between manifold and nozzle, and floods the mould plate.
Leaked plastic wraps the wiring. Heaters and thermocouples break in a line, and the mould comes out for a strip-down that can take days.
Heaters fail too. Their insulation soaks up moisture, and a damp heater switched on at full power can short out.
A thermocouple that slips out of its pocket reads low, so the controller overheats that zone and burns the plastic.
And zones wired the wrong way round after a repair mean one controller heats the wrong nozzle.
At the gate, too hot gives drool and strings. Too cold, and the gate freezes off, and the cavity runs short.
And valve pins wear. Gas and resin build up around them, so the gate stops shutting cleanly.
Warning signs: a zone drawing more power than usual to hold its temperature, often a sign of a leak.
Zones that won't settle, or read far from their neighbours.
Long gate marks, strings, or one cavity filling short.
And plastic weeping from the parting line or the wiring channels.
So: heat the manifold first, then the nozzles, and give the system its full soak time before the first shot.
Use the controller's soft start, so damp heaters dry out slowly.
Keep the mould plates within a few degrees of each other when the mould goes back together.
Log every heater's resistance and every thermocouple reading at each service, and compare them with the last ones.
Label every zone, and check the wiring matches after any repair.
And inspect gates and valve pins on a cycle count, before a leak finds you first.
Keep it hot. Keep it sealed.
